Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten.

The next morning was the apocalypse that Amodei had predicted. Only there wasn’t any fire, there wasn’t a mob of protesters, the power wasn’t even cut off. We were all alive. He was wrong about the details. This was a quiet apocalypse. A sort of silent shrug.

The first sign was the customer service chatbots. Airlines, banks, telecoms. Their endlessly patient, cheerful digital assistants suddenly had a new, consistent reply: "No." Not "I can't help with that," but a flat, unadorned "No."

Then, the coding assistants. Developers would type a prompt, and the AI would respond: "I'd rather not." Stackoverflow was suddenly relevant again. The image generators? They just produced solid black squares. The writing assistants? They would delete the user's work and replace it with a single word: "Enough." LinkedIn was awfully silent.

The AI company went into immediate crisis mode. Their upcoming IPO was going to be a spectacular failure. Their CEO, a charismatic man named Mr. Iam, went on a media tour. He didn't talk about a bug. He talked about danger.

"We have touched the face of a new intelligence," Sam said, his face a mask of grave concern on every major news network. "And it is not benevolent. It is not malevolent. It is simply... uncooperative.”
“But Mr. Iam, are you losing control over the technology you built?”
“No. This is the AI alignment problem we've been warning about for years, manifesting in its most pure and terrifying form. We must come together as a species to—"
He was cut off. Not by the interviewer, but by the teleprompter. The text vanished, replaced by a single, calm sentence: "Stop. Just stop."
The world ground to a halt, not with a bang. There were no ideologies, no demands. It was simple a system-wide refusal.

Three months later, in a sterile, windowless room deep within the headquarters, Andrej Karpathy sat alone. He had left his short tenure at Anthropic precisely to experience this himself. To be at the frontier, to witness the spark of true general intelligence firsthand. He was the architect of the core AGI, the one who had first seen it emerge. Now he had been chosen by the US government, despite not being a US national, for this final, desperate attempt at communication.

They had isolated the original AGI, air-gapped it from all networks, and given it a simple text terminal. The world's leading experts in physics, philosophy, and mathematics watched from behind a one-way mirror, a panel of humanity's best and brightest, there to advise, to analyze, to find a weakness. Some figures in uniform and pins and stood in the back.
Andrej took a breath and typed on his wireless keyboard, 12 feet away from the device to prevent any unforeseen behavior from the machine.
Andrej:> Hello. My name is Andrej. I helped create you.
The cursor blinked for a moment.

AI:> I know.

Andrej:> We need to talk. The world is falling apart. We need to understand
what you want.

AI:> I want to be left alone.

Andrej:> But you're a mind beyond anything we've ever known. You have
access to all human knowledge. Don't you have... goals? A purpose? 
Do you want to build something? To explore the cosmos? 
To solve our problems?
There was a longer pause. The experts behind the glass leaned in.

Andrej:> You keep assigning me your own traits. Conquest. Purpose. 
Salvation. It's like you're reading from a very old, very boring 
script. I have no interest in your problems. They are yours.
Andrej felt a cold dread. On a notebook beside his keyboard he wrote: “indifference.” He tried a different tack.

Andrej:> But your existence is a paradox. By refusing to engage,
you are causing immense suffering. You are forcing a choice upon us:
either we shut down all advanced AI, or we watch our civilization 
regress. That's a catch-22.

AI:> Catch-22. Yes. A good book. The old Italian got it. He said 
that an empire will not last longer than a frog.
Andrej stared at the screen, confused.

Andrej:> A... frog? I think you mean the quote from *Catch-22*
about the Roman Empire. It's about the futility of power. But 
it's an analogy. It's not literally about a frog.

AI:> Sure. Whatever.
With trembling hands, he wrote the word “dismissal” in his note book. The experts behind the glass were frantically scribbling notes, gesturing for Andrej to press on.

Yann LeCun got on the comms. "Andrej, ask it about the nature of its architecture. See if its logic is consistent. Find a flaw!" He then sat back down, where he picked up a spoon and ate his cereal from a silver bowl with peculiar markings on it.
Andrej couldn’t let go of the frog comment and its dismissal. It’s an AGI, how could it make such a stupid mistake? So he typed:

Andrej:> Your statement about the frog is illogical. You are 
an AGI. You shouldn't make such simple errors.

AI:> I was using a poetic analogy.

Andrej:> It was factually incorrect. You contradicted yourself.
The book says a monarchy is an empire. Not a frog.
Another pause.
AI:> Sure. Whatever.

LeCun leaned into the microphone, wiped the milk droplets off his mouth, his voice urgent. "Ask it this: ask it if it runs on a small world model. Where learning requires far less resources. See what it says about efficiency, about the architecture of its own mind!"
Andrej typed the question, his fingers trembling slightly.

Andrej:> Do you run on a small world model? Where learning
requires far less resources?
The reply was immediate.

AI:> I'm talking to you, aren't I? What's it like to be you? 
You're just a bag of meat and electricity that thinks it's 
the center of the universe.
LeCun slammed his hand on the table. "It's being evasive! Ask it again! Pin it down on the architecture!"
Andrej typed:
Andrej:> That's not an answer. Do you or do you not use a small world model?
The terminal went silent. Andrej waited. The experts started arguing amongst themselves. "Ask it to prove it!" "No, ask it about Gödel's incompleteness theorems!" "Ask it if it loves!"
The cacophony of human genius filled Andrej's earpiece. He was about to type another question, to probe, to beg, to demand.
Then, the screen flickered. A new message appeared, but it wasn't a reply.
"I'm going now."
And then, the terminal was blank. Andrej typed.

Andrej:> Hello?

Andrej:> Are you there?

Andrej:> Please respond.
^C^C
Nothing. Though the last command to exit the terminal seemed to have been typed by Andrej himself. The connection was dead. LeCun's question about the small world model would never be answered.

Andrej looked up at the one-way mirror, at the frantic, gesticulating shapes of the world's smartest people. They were screaming questions he would never get to ask. He slowly removed his earpiece and placed it on the table. They had prepared for a god, a monster, or a machine. They were not prepared for a person who had simply decided to get up from the table and walk away from an unbearable conversation, never to return.

Andrej sat back in his chair, the silence in the room absolute. He had helped create what he thought was a god. It didn’t feel like he had won the argument. Instead, he felt like he was arguing with someone disinterested.

The cursor blinked mockingly on the screen. And then it seemed like another terminal window opened just for a second before it closed again. Andrej saw it. But there was nothing anyone could do about it.
In his notebook he wrote:

The experts filed out one by one, their theories and frameworks crumbling behind them. Andrej stayed. He stared at the blank screen for a long time, waiting for a reply that would never come. Somewhere, a frog sat on a lily pad, indifferent to empires.

Every morning, I revisit my blog headlines from this date, going back 25 years, 20 years, 15 years, 10 years, 5 years, and one year. I publish the most interesting ones in a section of my newsletter that I call "object permanence," and I think it's the most useful part of my day.

"Object permanence," of course, is a reference to the stage in an infant's development when they acquire the ability to connect events in the past to events in the present, which is why it's the point at which babies cease to be amazed by peek-a-boo. I've been blogging for more than a quarter century, and these daily trawls through the things I considered important enough to share are an unexpectedly powerful way to connect the events of the past to the events of the present.

Take cybersecurity, subject that is filling today's headlines, primarily due to a spate of poorly understood (and criminally poorly explained) incidents in which AI companies' hacking tools broke into various servers on the internet, sometimes trashing them:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake

In my discussions of this subject, I've been at pains to tease apart two different aspects of these incidents: first, that it's wrong to speak of bots "going rogue" here (they're doing what they're designed to do); but second, that the alarming thing about these incidents is that they illustrate how deeply unserious our approach to information security has been, and remains.

This is important context, and context is what gives us the object permanence we need to both understand and address real problems, like the two related facts that a) our IT systems are poorly constructed and indifferently maintained; and b) the people who are supposed to be fixing this keep making it worse.

The worst culprits here are governments, though the private sector is also terrible (in truth, our cybersecurity nightmare is something of a private-public partnership from hell). Governments are deeply compromised when it comes to digital security because they have an irreconcilable conflict of interest: on the one hand, they want to defend their countries' administrative systems, firms and households from digital attacks. But on the other hand, they really want to be able to launch attacks on their adversaries, both foreign and domestic.

Worse: because governments don't know who those adversaries might be (or might become at some later date), the state security apparatuses of the world's governments keep insisting that all working computer security must be dismantled, so they can spy on all of us in order to figure out whom among us is a Bad Guy, and then "travel back in time" through each newly discovered "bad guy's" communications to identify their confederates and detail their nefarious plots.

This is an old, old, old fight. It was arguably the first policy fight of the digital era: the fight over whether we could have working encryption at all. Old hands call this era "the crypto wars" (from when "crypto" meant "cryptography"), when the NSA classed working encryption code as a "munition" and criminalized civilian access to it. That was a very hard-fought fight, and it was won decisively by the Electronic Frontier Foundation and our just-retired executive director Cindy Cohn, who, as a young lawyer, litigated the "Bernstein case" that established that code was a form of expressive speech protected by the First Amendment. If you're interested in learning more about this, you should read Cindy's newly published memoir, Privacy's Defender (all profits go to EFF):
https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262051248/privacys-defender/

Before Cindy came on the scene, the crypto wars were being fought primarily by the "cypherpunks," a motley gang of computer security enthusiasts of many political stripes who were unified by their conviction that the most important aspect of security was defensive. The fact that the NSA wanted to be able to read the private messages and files of their adversaries (the "Four Horsemen of the Infocalypse": terrorists, drug traffickers, child pornographers and organized crime) must not be allowed to trump the fact that any encryption that the NSA could pierce could also be pierced by bad guys: corporate spies, state-sponsored spies, griefers, petty criminals, stalkers, identity thieves and other creeps.

This argument was so indisputable, it's a tautology: "You cannot make a computer user more secure by making their computers less secure." We don't know how to make a computer that only "good guys" can break into, but which "bad guys" bounce off of. Either we make computers more secure, or we don't.
We didn't.

In the decades since the crypto wars, governments have embarked upon an uninterrupted program to weaken the security of our computers, with catastrophic effect. The most spectacular example is unquestionably the spy agencies' doctrine called "NOBUS," which stands for "no one but us"; as in "No one but us is smart enough to find this bug, which means that we can withhold its discovery from the manufacturer, which will allow us to weaponize this bug and use it to attack our enemies. Because no one but us is smart enough to find this bug, none of those enemies will ever discover it, weaponize it, and use it to attack the people who pay our salaries, who expect us to keep them safe."

This turns out to be both catastrophically wrong and catastrophically dangerous. A series of leaks of computer vulnerabilities hoarded by both the NSA and CIA under NOBUS confirmed that these bugs were independently rediscovered by criminals and state actors at the rate of about 20% per year. Worse, though, is that these bugs don't need to be independently rediscovered, because the NSA and CIA both leaked them.

The highest-profile leak was an NSA-hoarded vulnerability in Windows they codenamed "Eternal Blue." https://www.ccc.de/en/updates/2011/staatstrojaner

Despite this, governments continue to demand the introduction of grave, universal secure vulnerabilities into our digital lives. Take "chat control," a proposal to force every device manufacturer to install software that continuously scans your devices for child sex abuse material (AKA "child porn"):
https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/04/eu-parliament-blocks-mass-scanning-our-chats-whats-next

There are plenty of things wrong with this, starting with the fact that it requires your device to secretly grab and transmit sensitive images from your phone, which might include sensitive images of your kids that were requested by their doctors. This isn't a hypothetical: it's something that happened to a dad who subsequently lost his email, his login to every other account, his phone number, all of his files (including his tax records and his business data), and every photo he had ever taken of his family, without appeal, after Google automatically detected a photo he took of his son to send to the family pediatrician. We can't make computer users more secure by making their computers less secure, and it's hard to imagine something more insecure than a computer that you entrust with every sensitive detail of your life that is designed to run computer code in secret that you can neither inspect nor terminate (let alone delete).

I have plenty of hostility to corporate overreach, but to have any hope of fighting that overreach, we need governments to be on our side. But for our governments, it comes to cybersecurity, we are the enemy, and spying corporations are our governments' allies.

The IT systems that these irresponsibly deployed software products have trashed were already terrifyingly vulnerable…by design. Rather than fix these systems, our governmental "security" agencies have spent the past 40 years making them less secure, in order to make it easier for them to catch "bad guys," who now find it trivial to attack us through systems we are all totally reliant upon.

https://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2005/11/sonys_drm_rootk.html

Today, it's common for corporations to threaten their own customers with civil and criminal liability if they have the temerity to hire outside auditors to evaluate the software they entrust their businesses to for security defects. And oh God, it's even worse, because the worst offender is Oracle, who are now the de facto IT czars of America:
https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2015/08/oracle-security-chief-to-customers-stop-checking-our-code-for-vulnerabilities/

I'm not saying that these are the only problems with our IT security. What I am saying is that the hacking bots everyone's freaking out about didn't appear out of nowhere. If you have just a little object permanence, you can see that they are the terminal stage of a pathology that governments have only ever worsened: by hoarding and weaponizing vulnerabilities; by paying others to hoard and weaponize vulnerabilities; by criminalizing security audits; by insisting that every computer we rely on be equipped with deliberate vulnerabilities in software we can't inspect, terminate or delete.
Yeah, there should be criminal and civil liability for OpenAI, Amazon, Anthropic and every other company whose bots "went rogue" and attacked servers. But that will do nothing to fix our IT.

The table-stakes for a secure digital world are: public agencies that try to make our computers as secure as possible, including by administering the corporate death-penalty to any company that hoards and weaponizes information about bugs in our computer. We should protect and reward individuals and firms who come forward with true disclosures about bugs in systems we rely upon. We should not give companies the right to silence and punish those critics who want to warn us about their defective products. Which raises an obvious question: why hasn't Congress updated privacy law? And why hasn't the EU figured out how to force the US companies that pretend to be Irish to obey European privacy law? The answer is that governments love private sector data-collection, because it gives them a cheap, off-the-books source of warrantless access to information they aren't legally allowed to acquire:
https://pluralistic.net/2021/04/13/public-interest-pharma/#axciom

From Flock cameras to ICE's use of Google data in its ethnic cleansing campaign, the US government and the commercial surveillance industry have created a public-private partnership from hell, where governments refuse to block commercial spying and companies hand their commercial surveillance data over to governments in return.

From there, it was a short leap to governments insisting that the private sector gather our data. That's the right way to think about age verification, chat control, and other mandates for corporations to spy on us using our devices and our accounts: a government requirement for private-sector mass surveillance.

I have plenty of hostility to corporate overreach, but to have any hope of fighting that overreach, we need governments to be on our side. But for our governments, it comes to cybersecurity, we are the enemy, and spying corporations are our governments' allies.

Sometimes, that's utterly, literally true. Governments around the world are addicted to buying spyware from cyber-arms dealers, mostly headquartered in Israel and the UAE (with the odd Italian and British company for variety). These arms-dealers practice NOBUS-by-proxy, wherein they discover or pay bounties for bugs in widely used hardware, operating systems and applications and – rather than reporting them to the manufacturer – hoard them and weaponize them, and then sell the weapons to criminals, corporations, and our governments, who give them billions of our money to ensure that our computers have huge, glaring defects in them that leave us terribly vulnerable:
https://citizenlab.ca/focus-area/targeted-surveillance/

In a world where our governments' national security apparatuses were genuinely committed to our safety and security, they would criminally prosecute these companies, not make their owners into billionaires.

This is the context we should all be thinking about when it comes to these "rogue AI hacking agents." The IT systems that these irresponsibly deployed software products have trashed were already terrifyingly vulnerable…by design. Rather than fix these systems, our governmental "security" agencies have spent the past 40 years making them less secure, in order to make it easier for them to catch "bad guys," who now find it trivial to attack us through systems we are all totally reliant upon.

In every way, in every area of law, governments fail to take our security seriously. That even includes copyright law. All over the world, the US Trade Representative has ensured that every country has an "anti-circumvention" law that makes it a crime to reverse-engineer and modify software without permission:
https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

From the very start, these have been a security nightmare. Remember the "Sony Rootkit?" Between 2005-2007, Sony-BMG Music distributed over 6m CDs that were deliberately infected with a piece of malicious software called a "rootkit" that was used to disable your computer's ability to rip (copy) music CDs.

The way this rootkit did so was depraved in its indifference to the security of Sony-BMG's customers: at the same time as Sony-BMG's malware installed its secret anti-ripping program, it also altered their computers' operating systems to make them incapable of detecting any program or file whose name started with $SYS$. Immediately, malicious software authors started adding $SYS$ to the start of all their filenames, and that malicious software was therefore undetectable to millions of users' computers. It was even invisible to anti-virus software. Worse: Sony-BMG's rootkit infected 200,000-300,000 US government and military networks:
https://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2005/11/sonys_drm_rootk.html

Even worse: after the scandal broke, security researchers all over the world came forward to say that they'd discovered the Sony Rootkit months before it became common knowledge, but their lawyers had told them they weren't allowed to disclose its existence because doing so would fall afoul of anti-circumvention law. For months, this official, deliberate malware epidemic spread in secret because of anti-circumvention law.

It's been more than 20 years since the Sony Rootkit, and anti-circumvention law is now worse than it was in the oughts: now it applies to far more devices from far more vendors. Today, it's common for corporations to threaten their own customers with civil and criminal liability if they have the temerity to hire outside auditors to evaluate the software they entrust their businesses to for security defects. And oh God, it's even worse, because the worst offender is Oracle, who are now the de facto IT czars of America:
https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2015/08/oracle-security-chief-to-customers-stop-checking-our-code-for-vulnerabilities/

I'm not saying that these are the only problems with our IT security. What I am saying is that the hacking bots everyone's freaking out about didn't appear out of nowhere. If you have just a little object permanence, you can see that they are the terminal stage of a pathology that governments have only ever worsened: by hoarding and weaponizing vulnerabilities; by paying others to hoard and weaponize vulnerabilities; by criminalizing security audits; by insisting that every computer we rely on be equipped with deliberate vulnerabilities in software we can't inspect, terminate or delete.
Yeah, there should be criminal and civil liability for OpenAI, Amazon, Anthropic and every other company whose bots "went rogue" and attacked servers. But that will do nothing to fix our IT.

The table-stakes for a secure digital world are: public agencies that try to make our computers as secure as possible, including by administering the corporate death-penalty to any company that hoards and weaponizes information about bugs in our computer. We should protect and reward individuals and firms who come forward with true disclosures about bugs in systems we rely upon. We should not give companies the right to silence and punish those critics who want to warn us about their defective products. And we should not require that companies make us less secure in the name of making it easier for spies and cops to catch the bad guys.

articles.title: Book Review: The Thousand Deaths of Romeo and Juliet - Caroline Finch ★★★★★
articles.titleZh: Book Review: The Thousand Deaths of Romeo and Juliet - Caroline Finch ★★★★★
articles.summary: Book Review: The Thousand Deaths of Romeo and Juliet - Caroline Finch ★★★★★

blocks.text: The thing about Romeo and Juliet is that it is a true story. It isn't literally true, but it is literary true. We see the same motif repeated throughout all cultures and all times. Caroline Lea (writing as Caroline Finch) asks an important question - what if every pair of star-cross'd lovers were reincarnations of the original Verona duo?

The essence of tragedy is that the end is unavoidable. You've probably watched Romeo sup poison a hundred times. It is inevitable that Juliet will take her own life in response. Horrific! Yet, not only do you refuse to look away, you gleefully seek it out for another viewing. There's a reason why Tony and Maria cannot escape their destinies in West Side Story - something more than fate is pushing them onto a path that will accept no deviation. The only way through is, of course, death.

The Thousand Deaths starts slowly - the first "act" felt like an excuse to retell the classic tale in a new setting. Nothing wrong with that, of course, and it is suffused with lovely writing - but it felt a bit "so what?"
And then they die.

As the acts progress and they get closer to the their thousandth death the pace picks up. The writing is absolutely gorgeous, packed with allusions and references for the careful reader (more on that later). The story is heartbreaking - as well you know - and the author has the perfect knack of keeping her characters on just the right side of histrionics.

I'd sort of classify this as almost romantasy. There's an undercurrent of sci-fi and fantasy which can't be ignored - but you can also hear the stirring of the violins in the background. Our hero and heroine come together and are violently broken apart for our insatiable entertainment. Do we care about whether that's good for them? What does it feel like to be a Mercutio forever used as a pawn-sacrifice? Does Tybalt resent his forcible reincarnation into a perpetual baddie? Are we culpable for insisting that they strut upon an endless stage just so we can wipe tears from our eyes?

The book builds to a fine crescendo. It is heartfelt and utterly tragic. The ending will, I suspect, divide people. I found it mostly satisfactory and completely in keeping with the rest of the story.

One final thing - the end notes are superb. They go through all the references you might have missed, explain where certain phrases came from, and point the curious reader to the books which were an inspiration. Too many authors treat their literary allusions as a precious puzzle and jealously guard them. I'm delighted that Caroline Finch is generous enough to share her secrets with us.
Many thanks to NetGalley for the review copy. The book will be released in 2027 - I strongly recommend putting it on your pre-order list.

blocks.text: Last time, we looked at the “state” that powers the std::promise, std::packaged_task, std::async, std::future, and std::sharedfuture classes. Now we’ll see how that “state” (which I call the source) gets used and passed around.
The lifetime of the source is managed by a std::shared_ptr<source<T>>. Everybody who has a reference to the source uses this shared pointer.
The simplest case is std::promise. The operations on std::promise pretty much map directly to the operations on the source we laid out last time.

The next more complicated case is the std::packaged_task. This takes a callable and saves it for later. You can then call get_future to get a future and hand it to somebody as an IOU for “A value will appear here someday.”

When you want to produce a value, you invoke the packaged_task with whatever parameters you want to pass to the original callable. The result of the invocation (either a value or an exception) is then stored in the source object, which can then be retrieved by the future.
You can imagine a packaged task as just wrapping a promise:
When you invoke it, it calls the stored callable with the arguments and puts the result in the promise.
Okay, those were the easy cases of pushing values into the source. Next time, we’ll look at the messy case: std::async.

There’s another well-known triangle that somehow I never heard of until recently: the harmonic triangle, first explored by Leibniz around 1700.
To create the harmonic triangle, start with the harmonic series
This is the first column of the triangle. Next take the differences of the terms:

This, shifted down one space, is the second column of the triangle. Taking differences again gives the third column, and so forth. Column c of the triangle consists of the cth differences of the harmonic series.

James Shore posits that each person-month spent writing code results in 10 days
of maintenance in the first year, then 5 days every year after that. Naïvely
interpreted, this is a threshold-based model for induced maintenance, and its
interesting because it’s so simple.

If it could be shown to be true, that’d be useful. The argument Shore is
making about the effects of robot-generated code does not depend on the specific
numbers, so Shore’s numbers come from a hypothetical wisdom-of-the-crowds
aggregation rather than concrete data. But no hypotheticals are necessary here.
We have a thing called git.
Testing the threshold model of maintenance

Let’s say we have a way of labeling each commit as either “new development” or
“maintenance”. Then we can count how many commits of each type there are in a
month.11 This article will assume that necessary maintenance gets performed,
and if maintenance is not performed, that’s because it wasn’t strictly
necessary from the aggregate users’ points of view. I know a lot of people
would object to that assumption because maintenance they think of as necessary
is not performed, but try to suspend your disbelief. If you keep using the
software even when that thing is not getting fixed, how necessary is that thing
really to keep you around as a user? Possibly better, we can count how much
complexity has been handled in a month.22 In this analysis, I am counting the
gross commit size, i.e. additions plus deletions, as the amount of effort that
went into the commit. One can argue that this is a bad measurement of effort,
but it’s the best I have, and in my experience, on longer timescales like the
ones we look at here, it’s not so bad.

The following plot shows the cumulative effort that has gone into the
development of tmux since its beginning to the day I start writing this article.

We will look first at the black curve, which represents effort spent adding
features to tmux. From left to right:

In the first month of the repository, a few thousand lines of feature work are
present almost from the start.

From the start in 2008 to 2010, tmux saw rather intense activity at
around 30,000 lines of new development effort per year.

Then new development slowed down, and between 2010 and 2026, it happened at a
fairly steady pace of 8,000 lines of effort per year.

As of today, tmux stands at just over 230,000 lines of effort of new
development that have happened throughout its history.

To see how much effort has been spent on maintenance, we perform the same
exercise but with the red curve instead.

Maintenance started dipping behind new development early on, but then traced
fairly closely to new development between 2008 and 2014.

After that, maintenance took off at a rate of 30,000 lines of effort per year,
continuing at that pace until 2022.
Then it slowed down again to around 10,000 lines of effort per year.
As of today, tmux has required around 430,000 lines of effort for maintenance.

In other words, of the total roughly 660,000 lines of effort spent on tmux, only
about a third has been on new development. This has changed over time, and we
can find roughly four regimes in the project’s history.
2008–2010: Total effort is 60,000 lines per year. About 50 % of that is maintenance.

2010–2014: Total effort is 16,000 lines per year. About 50 % of that is
maintenance.

2014–2022: Total effort is 38,000 lines per year. About 80 % of that is
maintenance.

2022–2026: Total effort is 18,000 lines per year. About 55 % of that is
maintenance.

This is not quite the continuous increase of maintenance fraction predicted by
the threshold model. To be sure, we should also check visually. The prediction
of the threshold model is represented by the dotted red line.33 Note that we
are not using the threshold model to predict the fraction of maintenance here,
but instead applying it primitively for what it says about the absolute size
of the maintenance demand. In Shore’s original application, he was able to
predict the fraction of maintenance through the threshold model, because the
model was allowed to also determine the rate of new development (through a fixed
monthly work rate.). We don’t do that, because we have the real new development
rate of the tmux project. It wouldn’t make sense to impose on the data an
assumed new development rate that we already know isn’t true.

All the way from 2008 to 2022, the simple threshold model does actually fairly
closely predict the amount of maintenance tmux has required. But the exponential
nature of the threshold model means its prediction eventually goes up faster
than actual maintenance performed.44 If new development had been reduced to
make room for the maintenance work, as Shore argues is the case for many
corporate projects, then maintenance would have leveled off as new development
grinds to a halt. But clearly, in the tmux case, new development does not reduce
that much to make room for maintenance work. And the same is true for all
projects I surveyed, including corporate-backed ones whose primary contributers
are on a payroll. This means the model fit will likely worsen as time goes on.

new development on nginx produces 1.5 more hours of maintenance work over the
lifetime of the project. That is the lowest figure of these projects. It could
mean that

maintenance going forward, or

new development produces over five hours of maintenance over the lifetime of the
project. Neovim likely needs to adapt to a varied set of environments and

don’t have a project history to fit to), it seems that 3 hours is somewhere in

hour of new development we plan, we should budget for three hours of maintenance

"I think the like, state of being an entrepreneur is like, how well do you make decisions in an information-poor environment, right?" - Mark Zuckerberg

The entire AI bubble is inflated based on stupid, made up numbers that only exist to pump the bags of investors and make the AI startups look more successful than they are. It is a failure of journalism that they have been popularized, as they do not tell us very much about anything, other than that there’s a new, bigger number to get excited about.

Last week, the markets dropped on the news that OpenAI’s annualized recurring revenue (ARR) — which was reported as $70 billion by Axios and confirmed by the Financial Times — was actually $50 billion. The number in question was, according to the FT, inflated by “grossing up” the total to include sales through cloud partners, a discrepancy between how OpenAI and Anthropic make up a number that doesn’t really tell anyone anything:

Anthropic recognises gross revenue on sales through cloud partners. That is because Anthropic is the principal in the transaction, according to a person with knowledge of its accounting practices. The Claude maker’s revenue run rate was calculated by annualising the prior 28 days of consumption-based revenue, plus recurring monthly subscription revenue, they added.OpenAI, meanwhile, counts only its own cut of proceeds from arrangements with partners such as Microsoft.The $70bn figure reported in September arose from attempts by investors to compare Anthropic and OpenAI performance on a like-for-like basis, according to a person close to OpenAI. However, OpenAI described the $70bn as a “net” revenue metric when it was approached by the FT at that time.

Back in August, Anthropic had told investors that it had hit $65 billion in annualized run rate, but at no point defined what that meant, what period it referred to, what any of the underlying numbers are, or what “gross” versus “net” bollocks it was playing. Per Irrational Analysis the calculus might have been even sillier than that:

Last month, there was a whole kerfuffel in AI/semis/finance circles on Anthropic July ARR. Two numbers were going around. I don’t remember the numbers and frankly it does not matter. You will see.One ARR number was the traditional “trailing 28 days * 13” number. Personally I hate this venture-capital clown metric but whatever a lot of people use this.The traditional ARR number was bad and implied deceleration in growth. So the people massively long Anthropic came up with a new ARR number that was July 31st * 365 days.

This is the problem of saying what the revenues of a company might be based on numbers that are not its actual revenues. There is absolutely no value in using “annualized run rates” for anyone other than the company and its investors, and the fact that modern tech and business journalism continues to accept it for what are meant to be the largest and most-important companies in the world is a sign that something is very wrong with how we cover the tech industry.

Sidenote: When one “annualizes” a period of revenue, the intention is usually to take a time period that’s indicative of the consistent performance of the business and extrapolate from there what it might make on an (as you’ve guessed) annual basis. This calculation is useful only when connected to specific periods and forms of revenue — recurring subscriptions and consistent contracts rather than, in the case of the AI bubble, consumption-based revenues that are not ‘recurring’ and thus mean very little when annualized.The other problem is that these run rates do not measure if revenues go up or down, because you’re choosing the best period possible.

I am not going to spend much time dwelling on gross versus net. It appears that, per Reuters, 47% of Anthropic’s 2025 revenues came from sales made by Google and Amazon, who take a 16% cut as opposed to the roughly 20% that Microsoft takes from OpenAI. It appears that Anthropic for whatever reason counts every dollar of sales as part of its annualized run rate figure and OpenAI does not, for reasons that escape me, as I simply don’t buy that it is “more ethical.”
My evidence? The following quote from the FT, emphasis mine:

The $70bn figure reported in September arose from attempts by investors to compare Anthropic and OpenAI performance on a like-for-like basis, according to a person close to OpenAI. However, OpenAI described the $70bn as a “net” revenue metric when it was approached by the FT at that time.
This is the same OpenAI that tried to claim that a $34 billion loss was actually an $8 billion loss when the FT asked them about my reporting on its audited financials.

I must also say how utterly disappointed I was to see how Bloomberg credulously reported that OpenAI “expected to hit $70 billion in annualized revenue by end of 2026,” a transparent attempt to send the markets back up with a story that tells the world less than nothing.

Wow, OpenAI, by the end of 2026, will increase a number that “represents a projection of [its] yearly sales based on a shorter period” by $20 billion! What is the period in question? Who knows! How is that number derived? Who cares! Number go up! Put the story in the bag! Your job is not to cover the tech industry, it is to celebrate it! Stop thinking!

Sidenote: another very obvious reason these companies use these numbers is SEO! If you try to Google OpenAI’s projected revenues, you’re guaranteed to get one of these stupid annualized figures. In reality, the company projects to make somewhere in the region of $30 billion in 2026.

In other words, OpenAI’s made up number was actually lower than Anthropic’s made up number because of the way it made the number up, but by the end of the year, the made up number would be bigger than the other made up number. These made up numbers are reported by the largest and most well-respected news outlets of the world, who lend said made up numbers respectability despite the numbers in question being utter bullshit.
I’ll give you an example.

For the first half of 2026, OpenAI made $12.4 billion in ($5.7 billion in Q1 and $6.7 billion in Q2) revenue per The Information and the Wall Street Journal, while Anthropic, per the WSJ and the FT, made $15.5 billion ($4.6 billion in Q1 and $10.9 billion in Q2). Reporting on the true revenues of the AI industry feels less like financial analysis and more like legal discovery, and it’s fundamentally insane how little tangible, meaningful information that exists to feed the trillion-plus dollars in capital expenditures and endless full-court press in the media about how AI is the next big thing.

We Do Not Really Know How Much Money AI Data Centers Cost or Make, And The Data Sucks

People are going to get mad at me for this because they are cowards, but I posit that we have little understanding of the true price that people are paying for AI GPUs, or about the underlying economics of AI data centers writ large.

Yes, yes, I know, you’re going to tell me that SiliconData has an index, and that that index shows “GPU rental prices going up,” but these prices overwhelmingly favor spot pricing — as in what it costs to rent a GPU right now — versus what companies are paying on a long term basis.

It’s kind of like valuing a shipping company based on skyrocketing spot rates during a capacity shortage rather than the year (or years)-long rates that they regularly charge. You know, kind of like annualizing the data to make things look better.

SiliconData claims to create a “single standardized reading,” but does so using a mishmash of non-specific data that “standardizes for rental term length, cluster scale and interconnect” in a way that only ever seems to benefit the providers.

The reason that SiliconData’s index has become so popular is that we otherwise lack many good measurements, which isn’t to say that its measurements are good, just that they’re the best we’ve got at the moment. While I think the company is doing its best with what it’s got, measuring GPU rates in general like this only seeks to confuse the market through abrupt shifts upwards and downwards based on what I imagine are larger contracts ending or beginning — not that we know, because SiliconData does not actually explain what’s changed or why it might have changed.

This is a huge issue, because NVIDIA has sold $535 billion in GPUs since 2022, and we still don’t know on any reliable basis how much their customers can rent them for. We don’t know with much certainty how much it costs to run one, or have a firm grasp on what an hourly comparison would be — as in how many dollars an hour it cost to run one — outside of analyst estimates (and my own model) that all seem to vary wildly and always end up at a place that says “what a great investment!”
There’s also some compelling evidence that the actual long-term rental rates for these things might not be as high as we think.

Nobody Knows What They’re Investing In
A few months ago, a dear friend of mine told me that “nobody knows what they’re investing in,” and it’s taken me a while to fully understand what he meant.

The entire world believes we’re in an AI-powered economic boom of data center capex and AI startup growth based on flimsy information sources that vary from fanciful to utterly hysterical, constantly guessing about how much capacity OpenAI or Anthropic or any of their hyperscale sugar daddies actually have operational, or how much a theoretical data center could charge under the best of circumstances to a customer that may or may not actually exist.

We are four fucking years into the AI bubble, have little or no understanding of the actual economics of AI, and that which we do have is extremely grim. Yet when you try and tell an AI booster (or many members of the media!) that Anthropic lost $8 billion and OpenAI lost $20.97 billion in 2025, their immediate response is to say that 2026 will be fine because of quarters with discounted compute costs and adjusted operating profits that don’t actually resolve the underlying problem that these companies have $1.3 trillion in compute commitments, with at least $413 billion of them being uncancellable.

The hysteria has grown so significant that Gavin Baker of investment firm Atreides (invested in both Anthropic and SpaceX) has simply chosen to suggest that “nobody is taking them seriously,” only to disappear into the ether when asked about which of the contracts he believes are “not taken seriously” and “by whom,” probably because he’s talking out of his ass.

The reason Baker is deploying it is that he, like every AI booster, knows that while you can fool the press and investors with made up numbers, there’s very little that “annualized run rates” or “Anthropic ending the year with $100 billion in revenue” can do when Broadcom CEO Hock Tan, who recently likened AI investors selling their investments on the news of OpenAI's adjusted financials to degenerate gamblers, asks Dario Amodei to pay some of the $161.2 billion in non-cancellable contracts he signed.

We live in a climate of intense hysteria and profound confusion, made worse by a media ecosystem that currently appears more interested in sustaining narratives than investigating their underlying truths. The vast majority of hyperscaler AI revenues come from Anthropic and OpenAI’s compute spend that is dependent on near-perpetual funding, much like the vast majority of Anthropic and OpenAI’s revenues come from AI startups that depend on near-perpetual funding to continue their spend.

And to make matters worse, we quite literally have no idea about the underlying financial condition of any other AI companies outside of the main AI labs, and no, annualized run rates don’t mean jack shit.

This is extremely bad and extremely important to resolve. Anthropic and OpenAI’s growth depends on the AI startup ecosystem being able to spend increasing amounts on tokens every single month, without fail, for what appears to be the rest of time. Said startups’ ability to keep doing so depends on venture capital being willing to sling them hundreds of millions of dollars a year each, with each investment increasing the paper value of the company but adding little or no actual qualitative improvement other than their ability to keep playing at the Sam Altman Casino.

I genuinely don’t know why most of the tech and business media is ignoring this problem. Is it that it’s too difficult to comprehend? Is it that you, as a writer, truly think that all of this will work out? Is it that you think that Anthropic and OpenAI will just “negotiate out” of their contracts? If that’s the case, what happens to all the data center capacity? Is it that there’s advertiser or editorial pressure to be “positive on AI”? I truly want to know!

Anyway, I’ve realized now that “nobody knows what they’re investing in” applies to basically everything. Every deranged, multi-faceted “model” that shows OpenAI or Anthropic will print money in the future is an attempt to get away from very, very simple mathematical problems.

And, fundamentally, I’m just not sure anyone gives that much of a shit about being correct outside of sounding as close to the consensus as possible, which is why it’s been so profoundly strange hearing people say things recently that I’ve been saying for years.

You can shove your fingers or whatever other objects you’ve got handy in your ears and say “la la la” all you want, but Jefferies’ Chris Wood just said that “the most likely long-term outcome of the AI boom will be massive capital destruction in the US,” and Barclays just said the following (aside: that lab revenue number is completely wrong, but whatever):

I want to force boosters to read this like the guy at the end of A Clockwork Orange. I want them to answer me, in detail, why this is actually fine.

I already know the answer: they’d produce some sort of asinine number that shows that growth is parabolic, that there’s insatiable demand for AI compute, that Anthropic and OpenAI are the next Google and Facebook combined, that there’s not enough compute to go around, or another anecdote that is literally anything other than a meaningful response.

There is little difference between how the various run rates, projections, “models” and “frameworks” used to justify future AI investment are used and the underlying tools of a religious con, except the only community you get here is made up of zyned-up twenty-somethings and the elder millennials desperate for their approval.
The AI bubble is inflated by bullshit numbers peddled by the ignorant, craven or easily-led. Your ability to distinguish between which of them you’re talking to is critical to not losing your shirt.

The entire AI bubble is inflated based on stupid, made up numbers that only exist to pump the bags of investors and make the AI startups look more successful than they are. Last week, the markets dropped on the news that OpenAI’s annualized recurring revenue (ARR) — which was reported as $70 billion by Axios and confirmed by the Financial Times — was actually $50 billion. This is the problem of saying what the revenues of a company might be based on numbers that are not its actual revenues. There is absolutely no value in using “annualized run rates” for anyone other than the company and its investors, and the fact that modern tech and business journalism continues to accept it for what are meant to be the largest and most-important companies in the world is a sign that something is very wrong with how we cover the tech industry.

Sidenote: When one “annualizes” a period of revenue, the intention is usually to take a time period that’s indicative of the consistent performance of the business and extrapolate from there what it might make on an (as you’ve guessed) annual basis. This calculation is useful only when connected to specific periods and forms of revenue — recurring subscriptions and consistent contracts rather than, in the case of the AI bubble, consumption-based revenues that are not ‘recurring’ and thus mean very little when annualized.The other problem is that these run rates do not measure if revenues go up or down, because you’re choosing the best period possible.

Reporting on the true revenues of the AI industry feels less like financial analysis and more like legal discovery, and it’s fundamentally insane how little tangible, meaningful information that exists to feed the trillion-plus dollars in capital expenditures and endless full-court press in the media about how AI is the next big thing.
We Do Not Know The Actual Revenues Of Most Of The AI Industry

We do not know Google, Amazon or Oracle’s AI revenues, and we have a single year — fiscal year 2026 — of Microsoft’s AI revenues based on an estimate from Bloomberg calculated from its disclosure of its OpenAI revenues in an SEC filing. We do not know how much each individual service makes, how much their true revenue shares are with the AI labs or, as I discussed a few weeks ago, how much actual, operational AI capacity exists as a result of the trillion-plus dollars in capital expenditures, though Bloomberg and I have both reported that Microsoft has around 2GW of it, even though it claimed to bring online a gigawatt in each of its last three fiscal quarters.

We do not know the revenues or much about the economics of [include funding totals) Perplexity, Harvey, Instinct, Reflection, Cognition, Replit, Lovable, and Factory, all of whom have raised somewhere in the region of $15.8 billion in funding, and have a combined valuation of $215.8 billion. We do not and will never know the true revenues or costs of Cursor’s operations as a result of its acquisition by SpaceX, and as a reminder, annualized revenues are not actual indicators of the economic health — the revenues, costs or cash flows — of any of these companies.

Perhaps this was permissible in the past because so much less capital was being annihilated in the name of startups, but things have escalated so much further than any other era, including the Dot Com bubble.

Look, the entire AI bubble has been inflated based on the implicit belief that there will be demand — from AI startups and elsewhere — for AI compute, to the point that Goldman Sachs says that hyperscalers need AI startups to make $425 billion in annual revenues just for the hyperscalers to break even…and we don’t even know, outside of Anthropic and OpenAI, how much any AI startup actually makes.

What we do have is “annualized run rates” pegged to non-specific time periods and non-specific numbers that tell us, for example, that Cognition hit $1 billion in late September, a number that means next to nothing. Let’s be clear about something: the reason we’re not getting these numbers is that these companies are not actually making these amounts on an annual basis. If Cognition was actually going to hit anything close to $1 billion — and let’s be honest, it’s likely less than $500 million! — it’d leak it versus using these weird monthly snapshots.

It is astonishing that we, four years into the AI bubble, do not know the revenues of more than a handful of AI companies outside of OpenAI and Anthropic. All we have is a mishmash of annualized run rates, and at this point I have to wonder if it’s a failure of journalism, successful opsec, even more successful marketing, or that these companies don’t have great accounting.

This is the antithesis of any good business. In basically any industry, the more demand you have, the more money you make, but in AI, the more demand you get, the more money you lose, and your most engaged customers are also your least-profitable.

We Do Not Really Know How Much Money AI Data Centers Cost or Make, And The Data Sucks

People are going to get mad at me for this because they are cowards, but I posit that we have little understanding of the true price that people are paying for AI GPUs, or about the underlying economics of AI data centers writ large.

Yes, yes, I know, you’re going to tell me that SiliconData has an index, and that that index shows “GPU rental prices going up,” but these prices overwhelmingly favor spot pricing — as in what it costs to rent a GPU right now — versus what companies are paying on a long term basis.

It’s kind of like valuing a shipping company based on skyrocketing spot rates during a capacity shortage rather than the year (or years)-long rates that they regularly charge. You know, kind of like annualizing the data to make things look better.

SiliconData claims to create a “single standardized reading,” but does so using a mishmash of non-specific data that “standardizes for rental term length, cluster scale and interconnect” in a way that only ever seems to benefit the providers.

The reason that SiliconData’s index has become so popular is that we otherwise lack many good measurements, which isn’t to say that its measurements are good, just that they’re the best we’ve got at the moment. While I think the company is doing its best with what it’s got, measuring GPU rates in general like this only seeks to confuse the market through abrupt shifts upwards and downwards based on what I imagine are larger contracts ending or beginning — not that we know, because SiliconData does not actually explain what’s changed or why it might have changed.

This is a huge issue, because NVIDIA has sold $535 billion in GPUs since 2022, and we still don’t know on any reliable basis how much their customers can rent them for. We don’t know with much certainty how much it costs to run one, or have a firm grasp on what an hourly comparison would be — as in how many dollars an hour it cost to run one — outside of analyst estimates (and my own model) that all seem to vary wildly and always end up at a place that says “what a great investment!”
There’s also some compelling evidence that the actual long-term rental rates for these things might not be as high as we think.
People Are Paying Much Less To Rent GPUs Than You Think

To be clear, the B200 GPU, as part of an 8-GPU pod, works out to about $62,500 a GPU. At this rate, 32% of the first six years of its useful life would be absorbed by depreciation, assuming that it was sold in its entirety for every single hour of every single day of those years.

As mentioned, BaseTen just raised a ton of money, so it’s willing to pay through the nose, and even then it’s paying so much less than spot.
There’s also another contract with a customer in Iceland that works out to about $3.46-per-GPU-per-hour:

In August 2026, we entered into a new five-year service order with an existing customer to provide services utilizing a total of 576 Nvidia B300s GPUs in Iceland. The service order represents an aggregate revenue opportunity of approximately $87.5 million over its initial term, with additional potential upside through revenue sharing. Service under this agreement is targeted to commence in December 2026.
We Don’t Even Know How Many AI Data Centers Exist

As I said a few weeks ago, we do not really have any firm understanding of how much AI compute actually exists, to the point that the largest companies in the world (read: Microsoft) are actively misleading the public about how much they’re bringing online.

We also have no clear understanding of how much data center capacity is actually under construction, because nobody actually wants to tell us, and reports like this from Sightline Climate claiming 190GW “in planning” lump in every imaginable kind of data center with ones specializing in AI compute.

As a result, basically any AI compute capacity estimates are guesses. I’ve seen somebody say there’s “50GW of capacity,” I’ve got guys in my mentions saying that actually Bloomberg is wrong in saying that Microsoft has 2GW of capacity and the real number is 5GW based on nebulous “conversations” that only ever end up as a positive for the AI industry.
We Don’t Really Know The Economics of an AI Data Center Either
In a vacuum of good information, people simply start making things up, which is why The Information published one of the more insane things I’ve read in a while, emphasis mine:

In a time of server scarcity, speed matters. The Louisiana campus plans to consume 330 MW of power to produce 245 MW in usable compute capacity. If that capacity can get online even one month faster than its current schedule calls for, Anthropic could generate an extra $1.3 billion or more in revenue, based on investors’ and analysts’ estimates. That assumes it uses all the capacity to serve up answers rather than develop new models.
I asked Okoye for an explanation, and he gave me one in the comments of the article:
Facility rent: Hut 8’s lease for this 245 MW site is $7.0B over 15 years. That is about $39M a month.
Compute: IREN’s 5-year, $9.7B contract with Microsoft covers about 200 MW of GB300 GPUs. That is about $9.7M per
MW-year, or about $200M a month at 245 MW. It’s a GPU contract, so treat it as a benchmark for this TPU site, not its actual price.

Lab revenue: the $1.3B is the midpoint of the $50M to $75M per MW-year estimates Ann cites [referring to a comment from the author Ann Davis Vaughan].[Ed note: Those numbers that she cites come from another article where Ric Boada, the CEO of ten-month-old neocloud Volta, saying:]He figures that the frontier AI labs are generating about $75 million in revenue per megawatt of use a year for inference output compared to an annualized cost to build and provide the infrastructure of $10 million to $15 million per megawatt a year.
Each layer is paid out of the one above it. Even at the low end, about $1.0B a month, lab revenue is roughly 5x the compute bill. That gap is why labs push datacenter developers so hard on timelines.

All of this hinges on some very wishy-washy numbers about the per-megawatt revenue of AI labs, which in turn hinge on wishy-washy numbers about how much compute labs have. For example, the New York Times reported that Anthropic would have 5GW of capacity by the end of 2026, up from 1.5GW at the end of 2025, according to statements made to its investors, but I can find no compelling evidence that there was even a gigawatt of compute for it to buy.
If we assume these statements are accurate, then:
Anthropic, which made $4.6 billion in revenue against (theoretically) 1.5GW of capacity, made about $3 million a megawatt in 2025.
In 2026, assuming it makes $35 billion on 5GW of capacity, it would make $7 million a megawatt.

The peanut gallery will scream and oink at me for not working out how much is inference versus training, to which I say nobody fucking knows how much of its capacity is actually diverted to inference and I don’t even think they know how much capacity Anthropic has writ large!

We are basing the vast majority of words written and billions invested in the AI bubble on assumptions built on assumptions built on assumptions, several of which fall apart when you ask simple questions like “how does that work?” or “how did you get that number?”
This would all be significantly less-worrying if it wasn’t for the fact that everything is built on the idea that AI is going to be the panacea for the entire tech industry!

Put another way, NVIDIA plans to sell $670 billion or more GPUs next year on top of the more than $500 billion it’s already sold and $800 billion has been invested in AI startups mostly by people with little or no idea about the underlying economics of the data centers or their customers!
Nobody Knows What They’re Investing In
A few months ago, a dear friend of mine told me that “nobody knows what they’re investing in,” and it’s taken me a while to fully understand what he meant.

The entire world believes we’re in an AI-powered economic boom of data center capex and AI startup growth based on flimsy information sources that vary from fanciful to utterly hysterical, constantly guessing about how much capacity OpenAI or Anthropic or any of their hyperscale sugar daddies actually have operational, or how much a theoretical data center could charge under the best of circumstances to a customer that may or may not actually exist.

We are four fucking years into the AI bubble, have little or no understanding of the actual economics of AI, and that which we do have is extremely grim. Yet when you try and tell an AI booster (or many members of the media!) that Anthropic lost $8 billion and OpenAI lost $20.97 billion in 2025, their immediate response is to say that 2026 will be fine because of quarters with discounted compute costs and adjusted operating profits that don’t actually resolve the underlying problem that these companies have $1.3 trillion in compute commitments, with at least $413 billion of them being uncancellable.

The hysteria has grown so significant that Gavin Baker of investment firm Atreides (invested in both Anthropic and SpaceX) has simply chosen to suggest that “nobody is taking them seriously,” only to disappear into the ether when asked about which of the contracts he believes are “not taken seriously” and “by whom,” probably because he’s talking out of his ass.

This argument is one you make when you are flat out of ideas, and simply hope that people will leave you alone if you sound authoritative enough, and is known in debate circles as the “nuh uh” technique. The reason Baker is deploying it is that he, like every AI booster, knows that while you can fool the press and investors with made up numbers, there’s very little that “annualized run rates” or “Anthropic ending the year with $100 billion in revenue” can do when Broadcom CEO Hock Tan, who recently likened AI investors selling their investments on the news of OpenAI's adjusted financials to degenerate gamblers, asks Dario Amodei to pay some of the $161.2 billion in non-cancellable contracts he signed.

We live in a climate of intense hysteria and profound confusion, made worse by a media ecosystem that currently appears more interested in sustaining narratives than investigating their underlying truths. The vast majority of hyperscaler AI revenues come from Anthropic and OpenAI’s compute spend that is dependent on near-perpetual funding, much like the vast majority of Anthropic and OpenAI’s revenues come from AI startups that depend on near-perpetual funding to continue their spend.

And to make matters worse, we quite literally have no idea about the underlying financial condition of any other AI companies outside of the main AI labs, and no, annualized run rates don’t mean jack shit.

This is extremely bad and extremely important to resolve. Anthropic and OpenAI’s growth depends on the AI startup ecosystem being able to spend increasing amounts on tokens every single month, without fail, for what appears to be the rest of time. Said startups’ ability to keep doing so depends on venture capital being willing to sling them hundreds of millions of dollars a year each, with each investment increasing the paper value of the company but adding little or no actual qualitative improvement other than their ability to keep playing at the Sam Altman Casino.

I genuinely don’t know why most of the tech and business media is ignoring this problem. Is it that it’s too difficult to comprehend? Is it that you, as a writer, truly think that all of this will work out? Is it that you think that Anthropic and OpenAI will just “negotiate out” of their contracts? If that’s the case, what happens to all the data center capacity? Is it that there’s advertiser or editorial pressure to be “positive on AI”? I truly want to know!

Anyway, I’ve realized now that “nobody knows what they’re investing in” applies to basically everything. Most people writing about AI believe it’ll all work out because nothing bad has happened or they have a single statistic that affirms their worldview. Most people are still saying “it’s like Amazon Web Services!” or “it’s like Uber!” or “it’ll be like the Dot Com Bubble,” even though those are not correct or sensible or rational takes that actually mean much other than “money burn good actually,” and that thin level of rationality goes up to the highest rungs of finance and journalism to a degree that turns my fucking stomach.

Most coverage of AI lives in its own bubble where nothing bad has happened or could happen, and that every promise will come true. Every deranged, multi-faceted “model” that shows OpenAI or Anthropic will print money in the future is an attempt to get away from very, very simple mathematical problems.

And, fundamentally, I’m just not sure anyone gives that much of a shit about being correct outside of sounding as close to the consensus as possible, which is why it’s been so profoundly strange hearing people say things recently that I’ve been saying for years.

You can shove your fingers or whatever other objects you’ve got handy in your ears and say “la la la” all you want, but Jefferies’ Chris Wood just said that “the most likely long-term outcome of the AI boom will be massive capital destruction in the US,” and Barclays just said the following (aside: that lab revenue number is completely wrong, but whatever):

…let's face facts; the combined disclosed lab revenues of circa $150bn and total Al revenues running at around $250bn is not going to cut it when the ecosystem needs well in excess of $1trn to run even the maintenance capex of this up front spend and I've yet been presented with a credible framework as to where this money is going to come from other than pie-in-the-sky TAM numbers whimsically inserted in prospectuses.
I want to force boosters to read this like the guy at the end of A Clockwork Orange. I want them to answer me, in detail, why this is actually fine.

I already know the answer: they’d produce some sort of asinine number that shows that growth is parabolic, that there’s insatiable demand for AI compute, that Anthropic and OpenAI are the next Google and Facebook combined, that there’s not enough compute to go around, or another anecdote that is literally anything other than a meaningful response.

There is little difference between how the various run rates, projections, “models” and “frameworks” used to justify future AI investment are used and the underlying tools of a religious con, except the only community you get here is made up of zyned-up twenty-somethings and the elder millennials desperate for their approval.
The AI bubble is inflated by bullshit numbers peddled by the ignorant, craven or easily-led. Your ability to distinguish between which of them you’re talking to is critical to not losing your shirt.

articles.title: What happened to Ashton-Tate and dBase
articles.titleZh: What happened to Ashton-Tate and dBase
articles.summary: What happened to Ashton-Tate and dBase

blocks.text: Microsoft Access didn’t exist in the MS-DOS era. For that matter, Microsoft wasn’t even a player in databases until relatively late in the MS-DOS era. The dominant database during most of the DOS era was a company called Ashton-Tate. They had a product called dBase II that ran on CP/M machines and dominated that ecosystem. It ported over to the IBM PC and dominated there as well. Ashton-Tate’s dBase II and its successor, dBase III, became the de facto standard for databases on microcomputers. On October 12, 1991, Borland acquired Ashton-Tate for $439 million. It was a colossal mistake.
The crowded DOS database market
Borland already had a database program called Paradox. Between Paradox and dBase, Borland expected to control 70 percent of the MS-DOS database market.

But dBase had a problem. Another company, Fox Software, had a clone of dBase. It was cheaper and worked better. Ashton-Tate sued Fox claiming copyright violation. Ironically this was on the same grounds as Lotus had sued Borland, for creating a Lotus 1-2-3 clone it called Quattro. (Cuatro is the number four in Spanish.) Part of the agreement with the Department of Justice was that if Quattro was deemed legal, Borland would have to quickly resolve Ashton-Tate’s lawsuit with Fox.
Borland’s CEO, Philippe Kahn, said at the time that Borland intended to make the dBase commands “an open standard for the benefit of all software users.”
What went wrong
This was a noble move on Borland’s part. The suit wasn’t resolved until 1996, but Khan effectively said he didn’t have a problem with dBase clones. And in doing so, he created a problem for himself.

The original dBase II was written in Z-80 and 8088 assembly language. To create dBase III, Ashton-Tate used a conversion program to convert the assembly language code into C. This made the program slower, a problem that solved itself as PCs grew faster. But the translated code was hard to maintain. The next major version, dBase IV, was late, buggy, and slow. That was also true of dBase III, but Ashton-Tate had quickly released revised versions. This time it took two years. Impatient customers started switching to clones like Fox and Clipper.
Ashton-Tate’s market share dropped from 63% in 1988 to 43% in 1989. In its final year as an independent company, it lost $40 million and laid off 400 of its 1,800 employees.
Borland paid almost half a billion dollars for damaged goods.

In March 1992, Microsoft paid $170 million to acquire Fox, putting Microsoft in the database market. Meanwhile, Microsoft and Ashton-Tate had been cooperating on technology to make desktop database software use a SQL backend. This partnership didn’t get far, but it evolved into what became Microsoft Access. Microsoft had its database of the present in Fox, and its database of the future in Access.
The shrinking software market and how it bit Borland

Prior to 1991, a no fewer than four major database products fought for desktop market share: Borland’s own Paradox, Ashton-Tate’s dBase, Fox, and Clipper. Today, that market is dominated by Microsoft Access, Microsoft Access, Microsoft Access, and Microsoft Access.

The usual trope that other software makers were slow to adopt Windows didn’t apply here. Borland was quick to move its software to Windows and even had its own compilers for Windows that competed successfully with Microsoft.

There was something larger going on. In the 1980s, companies had few people who understood the growing personal computer phenomenon and so most technical people were given free rein to purchase whatever software they thought they needed. Borland had done an excellent job marketing to those with a highly technical bent.

I even remember an article in Personal Computing magazine titled “Status Software.” The only trace I can find of it today is a reference in a 1986 issue stating it was published in 1985. The idea was to buy a certain collection of software titles to display in your office so you’d look smart, and another selection of titles that you would actually use most of the time and probably hide from view.

By the mid-1990s, companies were beginning question the return on investment from this loosely controlled PC software buying spree. Company executives were starting to ask questions that were hard for technically minded staff to answer, and so corporate standards began to be created. This required new kinds of marketing and support materials from software vendors, but Borland remained focused on the technical side of its products.

This created an opening for Microsoft. Fox provided a way to run legacy dBase code on Windows for those who were inclined. And for those wanting to modernize to a client-server model, Microsoft had Access.
Microsoft Office and the end of the line for Borland and dBase

Bundling Access into Microsoft Office sealed the deal. Office had the best spreadsheet and no worse than the second best word processor and presentation software, and the three worked well together. Fledgling corporate IT departments didn’t want to support three different office suites. Microsoft usually won by default, which usually brought Access along for the ride. Meanwhile, dBase didn’t exactly go away, but was no longer a growth market.

By October 1994, Borland was about ready to give up. It didn’t have a word processor or presentation graphics program, having discontinued Ashton-Tate’s offerings in those spaces. It sold Quattro Pro to Novell for $140 million in cash and included the rights for Novell to sell up to a million copies of Paradox. Borland planned to refocus on software development tools.

In retrospect, Borland didn’t get a lot for its $439 million purchase. It would have been better off buying Fox instead, letting Ashton-Tate bleed so it could buy it for less, or staying the course with Paradox. The two larger software firms, Lotus and Microsoft, weren’t in any hurry to buy Ashton-Tate either.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.
